question: Cash payments of more than EUR 10 000 could soon be banned in the EU1, while cash payments of between EUR 3 000 and EUR 10 000 could require an identity check, and any suspicious behaviour will be reported. Brussels says that this is aimed at preventing money laundering.

Financial institutions, banks, property agencies, casinos and traders would play a key role in the fight against money laundering, corruption and the financing of terrorism. There will also be new rules for football clubs from 2029. The Council has stated that professional football – which attracts billions of euros of investment from third countries – is a potential vehicle for money laundering in Europe. 1.

Does the Commission believe that the EU institutions can tackle corruption effectively by banning cash payments of more than EUR 10 000, when those same institutions are directly affected by corruption scandals (Qatargate) involving socialist MEPs?

Is the Commission aware that the President of the European Parliament, Roberta Metsola, has promised that the EP will carry out an internal investigation to look at all of the facts relating to the scandal2?
Why is there a delay in these new rules being applied to professional football?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.4.2024) 1. The Commission has included in the anti-money laundering/countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) package proposed on 20 July 20211 measures to mitigate risks linked to large cash payments, in particular, by setting out an EU-wide limit of EUR 10 000.

This proposal has been retained in the final agreement struck by the European Parliament and Council on the future AML/CFT Regulation and complemented with specific requirements for operators subject to AML/CFT rules in relation to cash transactions above EUR 3 000.

The Commission believes that these measures are consistent with the purpose of EU AML/CFT rules, notably to prevent the misuse of the EU’s financial system for money laundering and terrorist financing purposes. These measures complement other initiatives proposed to tackle corruption at the level of the EU2 and specifically at the level of the EU’s institutions3. 2.

The Commission follows the developments and measures taken in the European Parliament. Given the organisational autonomy of EU institutions, according to which each institution is responsible for its organisation, definition of rules applying to its members and internal investigations, the Commission does not express any view on this matter. 3.

Professional football clubs and football agents are among the new categories of operators that will be subject to AML/CFT rules. Given the specificities of the sector, co-legislators have agreed to an additional two-year period before application of these rules to allow the sector to carry out the necessary preparatory work to be able to comply with AML/CFT requirements.
